title: Review: Second Largest Value
context: A teammate's single-pass solution to Second Largest Value, sent for review. The problem asks for the second-largest distinct value.

findings.title: A repeat of the largest value becomes the second largest
findings.explanation: A value equal to first isn't greater than first, so it reaches the else-if, where it is greater than second and gets stored. The answer must be distinct from the largest.
findings.consequence: Arrays where the largest value repeats get the largest value back. Public tests 2 and 3 show it: [5, 5, 3] gets 5 instead of 3, and [8, 8] gets 8 instead of -1.
findings.repair: Only take values below the largest: } else if (n < first && n > second) {

findings.title: -1 means "none yet" only because values are never negative
findings.explanation: first and second start at -1, which is also the answer for "no second value". That's safe because the problem says 0 <= nums[i], but a reader has to know that.
findings.consequence: None with these constraints. If negative values were ever allowed, -1 could collide with a real value.
findings.repair: Optional: a short comment naming the constraint, or a named constant such as NONE.
findings.why_preference: With the stated constraints -1 can't be a real value, and no test fails because of it.

debrief: One defect, shown by two public tests: duplicates of the largest value slip into second place. The -1 starting value is safe under the problem's constraints; suggesting a comment is a fair maintainability note, not a bug report.
review_status: Written for practice and machine-checked: the code and the repair were run against every test of the problem.
